archive.description: The archive to follow. Observe only reads it: it lists, and gets the objects and the catalogues beside them.

prefix.description: The prefix within the bucket. Required in a bucket shared with other installations: it is what keeps two of them apart.

batch.description: How many rows are written in one transaction. A transaction ends at an object's end, so an object is never split.

database.description: The index, as the role `audit migrate --observe` granted: read and write on the index and its cursors, and nothing of the deduplication table. Not the owner, and not the writer's or the query service's.

interval.description: How often a pass runs when nothing woke it. A lost wake-up costs at most this.

listen.description: A TCP listener. `address` is a host:port the service binds; an empty host binds every interface.

profiles.description: The profiles to follow. Unset follows every profile the archive has, found by listing.

settle.description: How far behind now the cursor stays. An object's key is fixed when its put starts and it is visible when the put ends, so a later key can be visible before an earlier one; this must be longer than a writer's put can take and than the clocks of the writers and of this process can disagree. It is the least time between a record's acknowledgement and its appearance in search.

wake.description: Where bucket notifications arrive, to make a pass run now instead of at the next interval. Optional, and only ever a shortcut: nothing a pass does depends on a notification, so a lost or repeated one costs latency and nothing else.

nats.description: A NATS subject carrying bucket notifications. Core NATS: the messages are not read, and one missed is the poll's to make up.

A NATS connection, and nothing else. What a service does with the connection — publish to a subject, bind a durable consumer to a stream — differs per component and is described beside it: a publisher with a `consumer` field it never reads is a field somebody will eventually set.

tls.description: Connect over TLS and authenticate with the service's own workload identity instead of a token. The certificate presented is the one the service's own top-level `tls` block loads (its mode must not be `off`); the broker maps the identity in it to a user with its own permissions, so what the service may do is the broker's decision and nothing in this file.
